assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin how central banks model and conduct monetary policy. Staggered pricing, the Taylor rule and the micro-founded policy framework are both a scientific advance and a major influence on practice. This is a field-defining contribution of very large societal impact.
assessment.attribution: The field has many contributors, so a three-person cap forces choices. Calvo is credited for time-dependent pricing, Taylor for staggered contracts and the policy rule, and Woodford for the integrated micro-founded theory of interest and prices. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler made important estimation and extension contributions that would go uncredited. Earlier prizes to Lucas, Sargent, Sims and Bernanke cover adjacent ground.
assessment.maturity: Decades of validation and use in policy institutions. The 2021-23 inflation episode tested the framework and prompted criticism, but it remains the workhorse. Timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a different three-person combination, for example Gali in place of Calvo.
Recent debate over the framework's performance during the post-pandemic inflation.
I am relying on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified attributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshaped international trade theory and empirics. They shifted attention from countries and industries to firms and explained who gains and loses from trade. The framework is a clear scientific advance with wide use in both research and policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extended it to exports versus foreign direct investment. Redding is a major contributor to the quantitative and spatial follow-on work. Krugman's 2008 prize covered the earlier new trade theory, and Helpman also appears in a separate candidate (Grossman-Helpman).
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation through extensive micro-data work. The framework is now standard in graduate training and quantitative policy analysis.
uncertainties: Whether Redding's contribution is better placed with the quantitative trade models in another candidate.
Possible overlap with the quantitative trade literature, which could blur the line of the discovery.
Helpman's cross-listing in B030 raises a question of how the committee would treat a single laureate across themes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combines a conceptual framework (skill-biased and task-based technological change, and the race between education and technology) with careful empirical evidence on trade shocks and local labour markets. This pairing of new evidence and an explanatory framework matches what the committee values. It explains rising wage inequality and has had large policy impact.
assessment.attribution: Katz, with Murphy and Goldin, gave the supply-demand framework for relative wages. Autor developed the task approach with co-authors outside the list. Autor, Dorn and Hanson established the China-shock evidence. Goldin and Acemoglu have already been recognised nearby, which makes the marginal contribution of this group somewhat narrower. Credit is spread across authors who are not all on the list.
assessment.maturity: The core evidence is more than a decade old and heavily replicated and debated. The task framework is mature. The China-shock magnitudes are still contested, but the core finding has held up.
uncertainties: Overlap with prizes already given to Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024).
Dorn is more junior, and the choice between Katz and Dorn is uncertain.
Ongoing debate over the size and persistence of trade-shock effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data transformed the measurement of intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects. The work links new data to causal designs and has had unusual policy and public influence. It combines data discovery with an explanatory framework.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leading contributor. Hendren is strongest on causal neighbourhood effects and on exposure-effect estimates. Friedman and Katz are important collaborators on specific papers. Chetty also appears in the public-economics candidate, which would raise a question of attribution across themes.
assessment.maturity: The main work dates from roughly 2014 onward. Replication and follow-up exist, but the long-run influence is still unfolding, and some findings, such as the place-based causal interpretation, are still being tested.
uncertainties: Relatively recent work, so the timing is less settled than for the older candidates.
Debate over the causal interpretation of area-level estimates.
Dependence on data access that others cannot easily replicate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Empirical optimal-tax theory built on the elasticity of taxable income, plus sufficient-statistic methods, connects tax theory to estimable parameters. It has strongly shaped tax policy debate. It follows Mirrlees and Vickrey but adds an empirical, behavioural dimension.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod is credited for early work on tax avoidance and taxable-income responses, and Saez for applied optimal-tax theory and evidence on top incomes. Chetty and Stantcheva each have separate large bodies of work and are left out under the three-person cap. Saez's inclusion also overlaps with the inequality candidate.
assessment.maturity: Roughly twenty-five years of work with ongoing methodological refinement. The taxable-income elasticity literature is mature, and its estimates and policy conclusions remain contested.
uncertainties: Contested identification in taxable-income elasticity estimates.
How much credit belongs to Feldstein's earlier work, who is not on the list.
Overlap with B018 and B045 through Saez and Chetty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Legal origins and investor protection created a cross-country empirical agenda linking legal institutions to financial development. It has had very wide influence across finance, law and economics, and development. The core insight is substantive, though the causal reading is contested.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are the La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny collaborations, so credit is shared among four people. Vishny is excluded by the three-person cap. Shleifer also has separate major contributions in behavioural finance that would complicate the attribution.
assessment.maturity: Work from the 1990s with abundant follow-up. Both the legal-origins thesis and its data have faced substantial methodological challenge and partial revision.
uncertainties: Significant critique of the legal-origins causal claims and of the coding of legal variables.
Whether the committee would weigh the framework's contested status heavily.
Potential for non-scientific considerations, which I do not weigh under the stated criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks (Kiyotaki-Moore) are a core mechanism in macro-finance. They explain credit cycles, and the mechanism was central to analyses of the 2008 crisis. It is a clear conceptual contribution with lasting influence on macro modelling.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the originators of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the financial-accelerator and empirical strand, and Gertler is also in the New Keynesian candidate. Bernanke's 2022 prize covers part of the neighbouring financial accelerator work, which narrows the marginal space.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of use. The mechanism is built into modern macro-finance and policy models.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize and with Bernanke-Gertler work.
Whether the committee prefers to include Gertler and treat the financial accelerator as the main contribution.
Limited direct empirical identification of the mechanism in the original work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantifying how misallocation of inputs across firms explains cross-country income differences is a significant measurement and framework contribution. It combines new micro-data with a structural framework, and it is influential in growth and development policy.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson's related work offers a parallel contribution, and Restuccia is on the list but excluded by the three-person cap. Credit also overlaps with earlier growth-theory prizes.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of use and extension. The interpretation of measured misallocation, including measurement error and the sensitivity of the results, remains debated.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of the measured TFP gains to measurement error and model assumptions.
Whether Restuccia should replace one of the proposed laureates.
Closeness to the growth prizes already given, including Romer and Aghion-Howitt.
